cases.abstract: Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT) learn multimodal continuous behavior from uncurated datasets by predicting learned action tokens rather than k-means action bins. Residual vector quantization represents actions or action chunks through coarse and fine codes; a transformer predicts these codes from observation histories, optionally conditioned on goal observations, and a continuous offset refines the decoded actions. Token prediction produces actions in a single forward pass rather than through iterative denoising. Across simulated manipulation and locomotion tasks, VQ-BeT generally matches or exceeds the tested transformer and diffusion baselines, with subtask entropy and multimodal rollouts indicating diverse behavior. Diffusion policies nevertheless perform better on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush. On a low-cost mobile manipulator under fully closed-loop control, the advantage is larger for sequential tasks: VQ-BeT completes 19/30 two-phase trials versus 11/30 for an adapted DiffusionPolicy-T, compared with 47/50 versus 45/50 single-phase trials. Onboard CPU inference takes 207.25 ms versus 5243.82 ms, reducing prediction cost when controller noise requires feedback at every policy step.
cases.results: On the real robot, VQ-BeT's advantage over diffusion is larger for sequential tasks than for standalone tasks. With all policies run fully closed-loop, VQ-BeT and an adapted DiffusionPolicy-T complete 47/50 and 45/50 single-phase trials, respectively, but 19/30 and 11/30 two-phase trials. Across four longer sequences, VQ-BeT's final success rate is at least three times the diffusion baseline's, reinforcing the distinction between individual task execution and completing a sequence. VQ-BeT also closes the fridge and toaster in both orders, retaining alternative task sequences rather than a single rollout mode. The hardware makes inference cost consequential: controller noise disrupts short open-loop rollouts on the low-cost mobile manipulator, requiring a new policy prediction at every step. Onboard CPU inference takes 207.25 ms for VQ-BeT versus 5243.82 ms for diffusion, reducing the prediction cost of fully closed-loop execution.

cases.abstract: Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) uses a separately trained imitation policy to supply candidate actions for both online interaction and temporal-difference targets. An off-policy critic compares imitation and reinforcement-learning proposals when selecting actions and repeats this comparison when bootstrapping, extending the role of demonstrations beyond exploration without a behavior-cloning regularizer. Keeping the policies separate permits different visual architectures: comparisons favor ResNet-18 for cloning but a shallow vision transformer for online learning. Actor dropout further improves sample efficiency. Under sparse task-completion rewards, IBRL learns faster than demonstration oversampling and regularized fine-tuning on Robomimic, while regularized fine-tuning performs similarly on simpler Meta-World tasks. Removing either proposal mechanism reduces performance despite retaining actor dropout, supporting their complementary roles in interaction and value learning. On real robots with manual resets, IBRL uses 30 demonstrations and 30,000 interaction steps to achieve 85% cloth-hanging success, compared with 65% for the reference cloning policy, 35% for regularized fine-tuning, and 15% for demonstration oversampling. Only IBRL exceeds cloning on this task within the tested interaction budget.
cases.results: On the real-world Hang task, IBRL improves on its imitation reference where alternative demonstration-based RL methods fall below cloning. With 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online interaction steps, IBRL achieves 85% success, versus 65% for the cloning reference, 35% for regularized fine-tuning (RFT), and 15% for demonstration oversampling (RLPD). Final checkpoints are evaluated over 20 trials per method using the same initial conditions; the hardware protocol uses sparse success rewards and manual resets. The 20-percentage-point gain over cloning measures policy improvement on deformable-cloth manipulation. Robomimic Square ablations distinguish this benefit from actor regularization alone: removing either imitation-based action proposal or bootstrap proposal reduces performance with dropout retained, and dropout-enhanced baselines remain below IBRL. Together, these comparisons support retaining imitation as a source of candidate actions during both interaction and target computation, rather than relying only on regularization or demonstration replay.
